bib.title: Model or Harness? An Interaction-Centric Taxonomy for Localizing Agent Failures

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: 50 of 50 pages extracted (159,899 chars). I read the body (pp. 1-13) and the setup text in Appendix A (p. 20) in full. I skimmed the reference list and the worked-example appendices (B, C) by keyword only. No extraction faults. No embedded instructions found.

FIT WARNING: this paper is largely off-topic for note 08. It is a failure-localization taxonomy, not a measurement of how much of a score comes from the model versus the harness. The text has zero hits for "maturity", "simplif", "observab" or "ablat". It gives no model-vs-harness score decomposition and no maturity stages. It is useful only for the failure-modes and fault-attribution part of the note.

SOURCE: "Model or Harness? An Interaction-Centric Taxonomy for Localizing Agent Failures". Harsh Raj, Vipul Gupta, Anas Mahmoud, Razvan-Gabriel Dumitru, Darvin Yi, Aakash Sabharwal, Yunzhong He (Scale AI). arXiv 2607.28802v1 [cs.AI], 30 Jul 2026. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

CORE CLAIM: Failures should be labelled by the interaction edge where they start (for example TOOL—MODEL) and by a fault side, meaning the component whose repair is needed. That separates model post-training, harness engineering, and environment or grader repair. It organizes 41 failure modes. Where several errors cascade, the rule is to label the earliest failure from which execution does not recover.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
All of these come from one validation. Four frontier models acted as agent-as-a-judge. Each had to recover the human label for 40 worked examples (public benchmarks, system cards, incident reports, logged trajectories) from the taxonomy definitions and a source reference. Settings: GPT-5.5 at xhigh reasoning effort; Claude Opus 4.6, 4.7 and 4.8 at adaptive thinking, effort max. Each judge ran a 3-turn session: evidence reconstruction, classification, reflection. The paper reports one set of results per judge, with no repeated runs and no confidence intervals.
- Human-label agreement on category (edge plus fault side): GPT-5.5 Cohen's kappa 0.76; Opus 4.6 and 4.7 0.71; Opus 4.8 0.70.
- Judge-to-judge kappa on category peaks at 0.84 (Opus 4.6 vs 4.8).
- Exact-match category accuracy (Table 2): GPT-5.5 0.80; the three Opus models 0.75. Full failure-mode accuracy: 0.72 (GPT-5.5), 0.70 (Opus 4.6), 0.62 (Opus 4.7), 0.68 (Opus 4.8).
- Given the human category, Opus failure-mode accuracy rises to 0.70-0.80 (Table 3).
- Selective voting (Table 4): 3 of 4 judges agreeing gives category precision 0.83 at 0.90 coverage. Unanimity gives precision 0.96 at 0.68 coverage.
- Structural count: of the 41 modes, 36 are model-attributable and 5 sit on other components. The authors say this is partly an artifact of their rule: "fault goes to the model when a more capable model could have avoided or recovered from the failure". It is not an empirical share of failures.

QUOTES
- p.2: "in a long-running Claude Code session an agent may ignore an earlier user instruction because the harness's context compaction removed it, or because the instruction remained available but the model failed to follow it. The observed behavior is the same, but the first case requires a harness-level fix, whereas the second requires a model-level intervention."
- p.3: "In one case, the tool wrapper suppresses the error, so the model never observes the failure. We label this failure TOOL—MODEL·fault:TOOL. In another case, the wrapper returns the error, but the model ignores it. We label this failure TOOL—MODEL·fault:MODEL."
- p.6: "We label the earliest failure from which execution does not recover" (stated as the attribution rule, "tracing the causal chain backward").
- p.13 (Limitations): "The taxonomy is descriptive rather than quantitative: it organizes failures and assigns responsibility but does not estimate their relative frequency."

Harness-side material worth citing (p.8-9):
- Context Rationale Erosion is attributed to the harness when compaction is harness-driven, and to the model when compaction is model-driven.
- Tool-side Mistranslation is the integration layer wrongly conveying a correct observation.
- Stale State Delivery and Service Failure sit on the environment.

LIMITS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT SHOW
- It gives no prevalence estimates. The 40 examples are "illustrative rather than exhaustive and should not be used to estimate the prevalence" (p.6).
- It never measures what share of an agent's score comes from the model versus the harness. It has no ablations and no interventions, and does not test that a harness fix or a model fix repairs the labelled failure.
- It covers no maturity stages, observability practice, or iterative simplification.
- The validation set is n=40, with one annotator ("the human annotator"), and no inter-human agreement is reported.
- Failure-mode agreement is weaker than category agreement. The paper says the judges may be hard to deploy in production.
- Some sources lack the evidence to pick a root cause. Example E4: 200+ emails deleted after compaction dropped the owner's instruction; this could be a context-side or a model-side fault.
- The authors worked on the taxonomy and judged it themselves, so a conflict of interest is possible.

BUILDS ON
- Barke et al. 2026, first unrecoverable event as the critical failure.
- Qiao et al. 2026 and Jorf and Shamout 2026, root-cause localization in traces.
- Cemri et al. 2025, multi-agent failure taxonomy.
- Zhu et al. 2025a, module-based error classification.
- Zhuge et al. 2024, agent-as-a-judge.
- Zheng et al. 2023, LLM-as-a-judge.
- Verga et al. 2024, ensembles of judges (selective voting).
- OWASP LLM and Agentic Top 10, 2025, safety-impact annotation.
- Anthropic 2026c, "Effective harnesses for long-running agents" (blog).

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 2 (p.7), "Interaction-centric taxonomy of 41 failure modes", a tree of edges and modes with shading for the fault side. Figure 1 (p.5), the radial interaction map, is the simpler alternative.

VERDICT: cite it narrowly, for the idea that identical symptoms can need a harness fix or a model fix, and for the earliest-unrecovered-failure rule. Do not cite it for any model-vs-harness score share.
